centenarians.text: In 1995, it was estimated that 1 in 50 Britons now in their mid-80s would live to age 100 or older. This figure is a result of improved nutrition and medical treatment which has improved for 1 in 16 for people in their mid-80s now (in 2010). Official figures showed this estimate for 2000 to be 1 in 25. There were 9,296 people aged 100 or over in Britain in 2008; an increase of 1,000 on 2007, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The findings come just a month after ONS data showed that there were 1.005 pensioners for every child under 16. In recent years there have been seven women for every man who have lived to age 100 or older, but this ratio is declining as male life expectancy is improving at a faster rate than that of women. The number of centenarians has increased by 5.4% a year since 2008 and this trend is expected to continue for the next five or more years.

What is the sum of the integers from 110 to 630?
questions.explanation: There are 630 − 110 + 1 = 521 integers with an average of (110 + 630) ÷ 2 = 370, so the sum is 521 × 370 = 192,770, which is under 200,000.

questions.text: What is the average of the inclusive integers from 162 through to 726?
questions.explanation: For a run of consecutive integers the average is the midpoint: (162 + 726) ÷ 2 = 444.

questions.text: A ladder 8m long is resting against a wall so that the foot of the ladder is 3m from the wall. How far is the top of the ladder above the ground?
How many tiles sized 20cm by 30cm are required to tile a floor which is 4 metres by 4.5 metres?

Imagine you toss a coin into the air and make a note of whether it lands heads or tails up. After 50 times, you have noted the following: Heads: 21 times, Tails: 29 times. If you continue to toss the coin a further 100 times, about how many times would you expect it to land heads up?
questions.explanation: 21 heads in 50 tosses is 42%, so about 42 heads in a further 100 tosses.

flag.note: The observed rate is 21 heads in 50 tosses = 42%, so about 42 heads in a further 100 tosses (A). PDF key C (63) is 42% of 150, the total number of tosses, not the further 100. Fair-coin reasoning would give 50, which isn't an option. The PDF gives no working.

questions.explanation: The differences run +1, +1, +2, +2, +1, +1, so the next difference is +2: 22 + 2 = 24.

questions.text: A bag contains 20 sweets, 10 of which are lemon and 10 vanilla flavoured. A sweet is drawn at random, and replaced, and a second sweet is drawn at random. What are the chances (probability) that both sweets are lemon flavoured?
questions.explanation: Each draw is lemon with probability 10/20 = 1/2, and the sweet is replaced, so both: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.text: At the local garden centre, pea canes have been delivered from the wholesalers in two batches. It was discovered that the first batch of canes measure 100.5cm, while the second batch measure 102.0cm in length. Given that the first batch is estimated to be the correct length, what is the relative error between the two batches?
A bag contains three balls, one red, one blue and one yellow. To the nearest percentage point, what is the percentage probability that the SECOND ball drawn will be yellow?
questions.explanation: Any of the three balls is equally likely to be second, so the chance it is yellow is 1/3 ≈ 33%.

questions.text: How many more Britons in a cohort of 100,000 in their mid-80s in 2010 can be expected to live to age 100 or older than a cohort of 100,000 Britons in their mid-80s in 1995?
How many more women than men were aged 100 or older in 2007?
In percentage terms what was the increase in the number of centenarians between 2007 and 2008?
questions.explanation: The increase was 1,000 on 8,296: 1,000 ÷ 8,296 = 12.05%, which is just over 12%.

questions.text: For every 100,000 children under the age of 16 how many more pensioners are there in 2010?
questions.explanation: 1.005 pensioners per child means 100,500 pensioners per 100,000 children, which is 500 more.

questions.text: Which of the suggested answers is the best estimate of the number of Britons in their mid-80s in 1995?
questions.explanation: The 1995 estimate was 1 in 50, so 9,296 centenarians implies about 9,296 × 50 = 464,800 Britons in their mid-80s.

flag.note: The 1995 estimate was 1 in 50, and there were 9,296 centenarians in 2008: 9,296 × 50 = 464,800 (B; F in the PDF's lettering). PDF key 516,350 (A; E in the PDF) can't be reproduced from the figures in the passage. The PDF gives no working.
